results.prompt: Compare the tiers and tell me the best value.
results.raw:
Here's a side-by-side of the three tiers (representative list prices — swap in your real numbers and the conclusion holds the same way):

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([cmp1, tbl1, row1])
cmp1 = Comparison("Tiers at a glance", [{name:"Basic",attributes:["99 kr/mo","1 seat included","5 GB storage","Community support","No SSO or audit log"]},{name:"Pro",attributes:["290 kr/mo","10 seats included","100 GB storage","Email support, 24h response","Shared workspaces"]},{name:"Business",attributes:["990 kr/mo","50 seats included","1 TB storage","Priority support, 2h response","SSO + audit log + SLA"]}])
tbl1 = Table("Exact numbers", ["Tier","Price/mo","Per seat","Seats","Storage","Support"], [["Basic","99 kr","99 kr","1","5 GB","Community"],["Pro","290 kr","29 kr","10","100 GB","Email, 24h"],["Business","990 kr","20 kr","50","1 TB","Priority + SSO"]])
row1 = Row([m1, m2])
m1 = Metric("Best overall value", "Pro", "Most capability per kr for teams of 1-10", "positive")
m2 = Metric("Lowest cost per seat", "20 kr", "Business — only if you actually fill all 50 seats", "neutral")
:::

**The verdict: Pro is the best value for most teams.** At 290 kr for 10 seats you're paying 29 kr per seat, and you get the things that usually decide a purchase — shared workspaces and real (if slower) support. Basic is only worth it for a single user; the moment you add a second seat you're paying more than Pro's per-seat rate for far less.

Business only wins on pure arithmetic: 20 kr/seat beats everything — but that price assumes all 50 seats are in use. If you'd only use 15 of them, your effective rate jumps to 66 kr per seat, and Pro becomes the smarter buy. The SSO, audit log and SLA are the real reasons to step up, not the discount.

Rule of thumb: **under 10 seats → Pro. 30+ seats, or you need SSO/compliance → Business.**

results.prompt: Show the costs and explain the largest one.
results.raw:
I don't have your actual cost data, so the figures below are an illustrative breakdown you can replace with your own numbers — the method of identifying and explaining the largest post is the same either way.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([g1, tbl1, ch1])
g1 = Grid([m1, m2])
m1 = Metric("Total monthly cost", "302 000 kr")
m2 = Metric("Largest post", "186 000 kr", "Salaries — 62% of total", "warning")
tbl1 = Table("Monthly cost breakdown (illustrative)", ["Post", "Monthly cost", "Share of total"], [["Salaries & contractors", "186 000 kr", "62%"], ["Infrastructure & cloud", "42 000 kr", "14%"], ["Marketing & ads", "31 000 kr", "10%"], ["Software licenses & SaaS", "24 500 kr", "8%"], ["Support & operations", "18 500 kr", "6%"]])
ch1 = Chart("bar", "Cost by post (kr per month)", ["Salaries", "Infra", "Marketing", "Licenses", "Support"], [{name: "Cost", values: [186000, 42000, 31000, 24500, 18500]}])
:::

**The largest cost is salaries and contractors, at about 62% of the total.**

Why it dominates:

- **It scales with time, not usage.** Every month of engineering or consulting time is paid for whether the product ships or not. Infrastructure, by contrast, only grows when traffic or data grows.
- **It is the only post that is an order of magnitude bigger.** Cutting *all* infrastructure spend to zero would free 42 000 kr. Trimming one full-time role frees more than that.
- **It is the least compressible per unit.** Licenses can be downgraded and ads paused within a day; headcount commitments take weeks to months to unwind.

Practical levers, in rough order of impact:

1. **Scope, then headcount** — removing a workstream removes the people needed for it. This is the only lever that moves the number materially.
2. **Change the mix** — shift some work to fixed-price contractors or lower-cost regions; keeps capability without permanent burn.
3. **Then software and marketing** — together they are only ~18% of the total, so they are tuning, not restructuring.
4. **Last, infrastructure** — optimise it for margin hygiene, not for savings; its ceiling is 14%.

If you paste your real cost lines (post, amount, period), I'll rebuild the table and chart and identify the true largest driver with its share.

results.prompt: Chart the growth and interpret it.
results.raw:
Growth here is steady compounding rather than a spike-and-dip pattern — that's the story worth reading from the shape.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([m1, g1, d1, tl1])
m1 = Metric("Revenue CAGR", "25.6%", "2019–2025, six full years", "positive")
g1 = Grid([ch1, ch2])
ch1 = Chart("line", "Revenue, indexed level", ["2019","2020","2021","2022","2023","2024","2025"], [{name:"Revenue (M kr)", values:[12,15,19,24,30,38,47]}])
ch2 = Chart("bar", "Year-over-year growth", ["2020","2021","2022","2023","2024","2025"], [{name:"YoY growth (%)", values:[25.0,26.7,26.3,25.0,26.7,23.7]}])
d1 = Divider()
tl1 = Timeline("What the shape implies", [{title:"2020–2023: stable base", description:"Growth stays in a narrow 25–27% band — expansion looks repeatable, not event-driven.", status:"done"},{title:"2024: local peak", description:"26.7% marks the strongest year; capacity and hiring are likely at their most stretched here.", status:"done"},{title:"2025: first deceleration", description:"23.7% is the weakest year in the series — an inflection worth explaining before projecting forward.", status:"active"}])
:::

**Reading it:** the line bends upward smoothly with no plateau, so the ~25.6% CAGR is a genuine compounding trend rather than one outlier year carrying the rest. The bar chart is the more diagnostic view: growth is remarkably constant for four years, then slips in 2025.

**Interpretation and caveat:** constant percentage growth means absolute additions are growing fast (about 5M kr added in 2025 versus 3M in 2020) — that gets harder to sustain mechanically as the base grows. The 2025 dip is small, but it is the first one; if it continues, a straight-line forecast will overshoot. If you give me the actual figures plus drivers (price vs. volume, churn), I'll re-chart it and separate real growth from pricing effects.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}

$height = 175
$weight = 75
bmi = $weight / (($height / 100) * ($height / 100))
category = $bmi < 18.5 ? "Underweight" : $bmi < 25 ? "Normal weight" : $bmi < 30 ? "Overweight" : "Obese"
tone = $bmi < 18.5 ? "warning" : $bmi < 25 ? "positive" : $bmi < 30 ? "warning" : "negative"

BMI is only a rough screening number — it doesn't distinguish muscle from fat, and waist circumference, body composition and fitness matter just as much. If the result lands outside the normal band and you want to act on it, the usual next step is a check of waist measurement and a talk with a clinician rather than chasing the BMI number itself.

results.prompt: Build a custom 3D bar chart you can spin.
Make a loan calculator with sliders.
Compare AWS vs GCP vs Azure.
results.raw:
All three are credible general-purpose clouds; the real difference is where each one's center of gravity sits and how it fits your existing stack.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([cmp1, tbl1, ch1])
cmp1 = Comparison("Where each cloud is strongest", [{name:"AWS",attributes:["Broadest service catalog","Largest ecosystem and talent pool","Deepest compliance and region coverage","Default, low-risk choice"]},{name:"Azure",attributes:["Best fit for Microsoft estates","Strong hybrid story (Arc, Stack)","Enterprise agreements and licensing","Win in Windows/.NET/Entra shops"]},{name:"GCP",attributes:["Best data and AI foundations","Cleanest Kubernetes pedigree","Simple, transparent pricing","Smaller ecosystem and enterprise footprint"]}])
tbl1 = Table("Side by side", ["Dimension","AWS","Azure","GCP"], [["Est. share of cloud spend","~30%","~21%","~12%"],["Primary fit","Breadth, startups to enterprise","Microsoft-centric enterprises","Data, AI, digital-native"],["Data & analytics","Broad but assembly required","Fabric, Synapse","BigQuery — best in class"],["AI / ML","Bedrock, SageMaker","Azure OpenAI, Foundry","Vertex, Gemini, TPUs"],["Containers","EKS — mature, configurable","AKS — good, tight with AD","GKE — strongest Kubernetes"],["Hybrid / on-prem","Outposts, limited","Strongest (Arc, Stack)","Anthos, niche"],["Pricing model","Complex, discounts at scale","EA/licensing driven","Transparent, sustained-use discounts"],["Regions","Most regions and AZs","Broad, strong in regulated markets","Fewest regions"],["Main weakness","Complexity, egress costs","Licensing traps, slower innovation","Smallest ecosystem, enterprise gaps"]])
ch1 = Chart("bar", "Estimated share of global cloud infrastructure spend", ["AWS","Azure","GCP"], [{name:"Share (%)", values:[30,21,12]}])
:::

How to read this: analyst estimates for share vary by methodology, so treat the chart as direction, not gospel.

Practical guidance:

- **Already on Microsoft** (Entra ID, Windows Server, M365, .NET) → Azure usually wins on integration and licensing, even when raw compute is cheaper elsewhere.
- **Data- or AI-heavy workloads** → GCP is often the best technical choice (BigQuery, Vertex, TPUs), especially for greenfield work.
- **Anything else, or uncertain** → AWS is the safe default: the widest service menu, the largest hiring pool, and the most third-party tooling that assumes it first.
- **Real-world answer** → most mid-size and large companies run two of the three. Multi-cloud is common; picking a primary and being disciplined about it matters more than the logo.

results.raw:
Cities can be ranked two ways — by **urban area** (the built-up agglomeration) or by **city proper** (the administrative boundary). The two lists differ a lot, so here is the standard "urban area" ranking, with the city-proper figure alongside for contrast:

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}

:::

Two things worth knowing: on the city-proper measure the leader is **Chongqing, China** (~32M), because its municipal boundary covers a huge rural area — which is why most demographers prefer the urban-area definition. And Tokyo's lead is narrowing: by 2030 Delhi is projected to overtake it as the world's largest urban area.

Figures are UN World Urbanization Prospects estimates and rounded; different sources vary by a few million depending on where they draw the metro boundary.

Send me the details (a document, a set of specs, a project status, a comparison) and I'll split them into meaningful tabs — or say the word if you'd rather have a single table or chart instead.

results.prompt: Create a survey form with a rating.
results.raw:
Here's a ready-to-use satisfaction survey — rating, NPS slider, and free-text feedback, all live.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([form1, row1])
$name = ""
$rating = "4 stars"
$feature = "Onboarding"
$nps = 8
$contact = false
$comments = ""
form1 = Form("Customer satisfaction survey", [f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6, btnRow])
f1 = Field("Your name", [i1], "Optional — we only use it if you ask for a reply")
i1 = Input("Name", $name, "e.g. Anna")
f2 = Field("Overall rating", [r1], "1 star = poor, 5 stars = excellent")
r1 = Radio("How would you rate us?", $rating, ["5 stars", "4 stars", "3 stars", "2 stars", "1 star"])
f3 = Field("Most used feature", [sel1])
sel1 = Select("Feature", $feature, ["Onboarding", "Dashboard", "Reports", "Integrations", "Support"])
f4 = Field("How likely are you to recommend us?", [sl1, p1], "0 = not at all, 10 = very likely")
sl1 = Slider("Score", $nps, 0, 10, 1)
p1 = Progress("Recommend score", $nps * 10)
f5 = Field("Can we contact you?", [sw1])
sw1 = Switch("Yes, follow up with me", $contact)
f6 = Field("Anything else?", [t1])
t1 = Textarea("Comments", $comments, "What worked, what didn't?")
btnRow = Row([b1, b2])
b1 = Button("Submit feedback", "notes.create", {title:"Survey feedback", content:"Customer satisfaction survey response"})
b2 = Button("Clear comments", @Reset($comments))
row1 = Row([m1, m2])
m1 = Metric("Rating", $rating, "Overall satisfaction")
m2 = Metric("Recommend score", $nps, "NPS 0-10", "positive")
:::

The numeric answers update the two metrics above as you move the slider or pick a rating, so respondents get instant feedback. Submit saves the response; swap the action id for your own endpoint if you're collecting into a backend.

results.prompt: Explain the water cycle.
results.raw:
The water cycle is Earth's continuous circulation of water between the ocean, atmosphere, land, and living things. Water is neither created nor destroyed in it — it only changes state (liquid ↔ vapor ↔ ice) and location. Solar energy and gravity are the two forces driving the whole system.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Table("The stages, in order", ["Stage", "What happens", "Driver"], rows)
rows = [["Evaporation", "Liquid water at ocean, lake, and soil surfaces turns to vapor; roughly 86% of global evaporation comes from the oceans", "Solar radiation"], ["Transpiration", "Plants release vapor through leaf pores; together with surface evaporation this is called evapotranspiration", "Sunlight and plant physiology"], ["Condensation", "Rising vapor cools and condenses onto dust and aerosol particles, forming cloud droplets", "Cooling with altitude"], ["Precipitation", "Droplets grow heavy enough to fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail; about 78% falls straight back onto the ocean", "Gravity"], ["Runoff and streams", "Water on land flows downhill through rivers and lakes and eventually returns to the sea", "Gravity and topography"], ["Infiltration and groundwater", "Water soaks into soil and rock, recharging aquifers where it can be stored for years or millennia", "Permeability and gravity"], ["Storage (ice, snow, lakes)", "Water is held for varying periods in glaciers, snowpack, lakes, and the deep ocean before returning to the cycle", "Temperature and geography"]]
:::

**Two numbers worth remembering.** The atmosphere holds only about 0.001% of Earth's water at any moment, yet that water is completely replaced roughly every 8–9 days — the atmosphere is a small but extremely fast-moving reservoir. By contrast, water in the deep ocean or a large glacier may sit there for thousands of years before completing a single trip through the cycle.

**What it means in practice.** Because the cycle is a closed loop of total water but an open loop of *fresh* water, the amount of usable freshwater depends on how often precipitation falls over land versus how fast it runs off or evaporates. Warming the planet speeds up evaporation and lets the atmosphere hold more vapor, which intensifies both heavy rainfall and drought — the same cycle, running with more energy. Groundwater is the slowest part of the loop, which is why aquifers depleted by pumping can take centuries to refill.
